response.guard_reason: no_canonical (rule: subject has no defined canonical; abstaining)
response.explain_guard: 'temp' names a measurement but no subject, so there is no one field it can mean -- a tag called 'temp' could be coolant, spindle, ambient or hydraulic, and Forge will not pick for you. Nothing is wrong with the value. The reading is returned unchanged under 'temp' and no value was altered or dropped. To map it, send a qualified tag name (for example 'coolant_temp' rather than 'temp'), or declare the mapping for this OEM.

'coolant_temp' matched only 'vehicle.ambient.air_temp', which belongs to the vehicle vertical, and this machine is cnc. Forge refused rather than store a cnc reading in a vehicle field. THIS IS A COVERAGE GAP, NOT A BAD READING: the value is plausible and nothing about it was rejected. The reading is returned unchanged under 'coolant_temp' and no value was altered or dropped. If 'coolant_temp' has an equivalent on the cnc vertical, it is not aliased yet -- that alias is the fix. If the machine really is vehicle, pass the matching `oem` so the right pack is used.

'wind_speed' looks like a linear_speed measurement and the only candidate 'speed_rpm' measures rotational_speed. Mapping it would have stored a linear_speed value in a rotational_speed field, which is a silent unit error -- the kind nothing downstream can detect -- so Forge refused. The reading itself is fine. The reading is returned unchanged under 'wind_speed' and no value was altered or dropped. Name the quantity in the tag name and it resolves: a tag ending in '_linear_speed' maps where 'wind_speed' cannot. Otherwise declare the mapping for this OEM.

'S1_CommandVelocity' names the spindle and the only candidate 'axes.x_velocity_commanded' is a linear-axis field. Same vertical, different subject: the value is a real spindle reading and storing it on the linear-axis would attribute it to the wrong part of the machine. Nothing is wrong with the value. The reading is returned unchanged under 'S1_CommandVelocity' and no value was altered or dropped. If the tag really is a linear-axis reading, drop the spindle prefix; otherwise request the spindle canonical.

9999 is far outside the plausible band for level_pct (plausible level_pct readings fall within 0 to 150), which is what the only candidate 'level_pct' measures, so Forge refused the mapping. THIS IS NOT A CLAIM THAT YOUR SENSOR IS WRONG. A value this far out usually means 'CoolantLevel' is not a level_pct at all -- a fault sentinel like 9999, a raw counter, or a different unit -- and the guard is telling you the CANDIDATE is wrong, not the reading. The reading is returned unchanged under 'CoolantLevel' and no value was altered or dropped. If 'CoolantLevel' is a different quantity, name it in the tag; if it is a sentinel, filter it upstream.
